<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  **Time:** ~15 minutes.<br>
  **Data:** a saved SIRUP object of the example MG thymus data, with BCRs, TCRs, gene expression, and cell-type estimates.<br>
  **Needs:** SIRUP with spdep, scoper, and spatstat.explore, spatstat.geom, and spatstat.random.
</div>

Here, we will test whether genes, cell types, and clones form spatial patterns in one myasthenia gravis (MG) thymus section.

A map can suggest that a gene clusters or that a clone stays in one place, and a spatial statistic tests whether the pattern is stronger than chance.
We will run five tests, plus one description of how far clones spread:

| Question | Function | Statistic |
|---|---|---|
| Is a variable spatially autocorrelated? | `spatialMoran()` | Global Moran's I |
| Where is a variable spatially autocorrelated? | `spatialLocalMoran()` | Local Moran's I |
| Do two variables co-vary in space? | `spatialLee()` | Lee's L |
| Do two spot types sit near each other? | `spatialRipleyCrossK()` | Ripley's cross K |
| Is a clone spatially autocorrelated? | `spatialCloneJoinCount()` | Join count |
| How far does a clone spread? | `spatialCloneSpread()` | Pairwise distances |

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  This page starts with a saved SIRUP object, which is loaded below. To learn how the object is built, see `vignette("get-started", package = "SIRUP")`. To decide which test to use, see `vignette("choose-spatial-statistic", package = "SIRUP")`.
</div>

## Load the example object

This code downloads a saved SIRUP object for one MG thymus section, which is not part of the SIRUP package, and reads it. The object has a BCR slot and a TCR slot,
the cell-type proportions in the Seurat metadata (estimated with cell2location), and BCR clones. Change `dest` to a folder you want to keep. The function skips files that are
already there. Each function on this page accepts a SIRUP object and reads the spot coordinates and the image settings from it. To see how the object was built, see
`vignette("get-started", package = "SIRUP")`.

```{r download-data}
extdata <- SIRUP::downloadSIRUPExample(
  dest = file.path(tempdir(), "SIRUP_example"),
  files = "mg_thymus_slice2.sirup.rds"
)
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(SIRUP)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

sirup <- readSIRUP(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2.sirup.rds"))
sirup
```

## Choose the neighbors

Most of these statistics compare each spot with its neighbors. The neighbors are chosen in one of two ways:

* `k` sets the `k` nearest spots as neighbors. Use `k = 6` for standard Visium, where each spot has six neighbors on a hexagonal grid. Use `k = 8` for
  Visium HD, where each bin has eight neighbors on a square grid. A larger `k` measures patterns over larger distances.
* `radius` sets all spots within a distance as neighbors. SIRUP measures distances in image pixels at the stored `image_scale`, so the same distance in
  micrometers needs a different number at `"lowres"` and at `"hires"`.

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Tip</b> </p>
  `k` does not depend on the image scale, so it is a good default.
</div>

## Test whether a variable is spatially autocorrelated

Use `spatialMoran()` to determine if a continuous variable is spatially autocorrelated, i.e., if neighboring spots have similar values. This function
computes [Moran's I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moran%27s_I#Global_Moran's_I). Moran's I is near 0 when the values show no spatial pattern, it is positive
when similar values are nearby, and it is negative when dissimilar values are nearby.

`variable_type` tells the function what type of variable it is:

* `"feature"` is a gene, from the assay and layer that are given.
* `"metadata"` is a numeric spot metadata column. For a text column, give `value` to test the spots that have that value.
* `"receptor"` is 1 for spots with any receptor and 0 for other spots. `variable` is a label only.
* `"clone"` is 1 for spots with the clone that `variable` names.

This chunk tests *AICDA*, a marker of germinal center B cells:

```{r moran}
aicda <- spatialMoran(
  sirup,
  variable = "AICDA",
  variable_type = "feature",
  assay = "Spatial",
  layer = "data",
  k = 6
)
aicda$test
```

The result is a list, and `test` is the `spdep::moran.test()` result. It holds the statistic, its expected value under no spatial pattern, the variance, and the p value.
For *AICDA*, $I$ is small, about 0.06, and the p value is below $10^{-9}$. The assay detects *AICDA* in few spots, and most spots have a count of zero. The clustering is
weak, but chance is a poor explanation for it. $I$ gives the size of the pattern and the p value gives the evidence for it.

The same function tests cell-type proportions and receptor presence:

```{r moran-more}
moran_table <- bind_rows(
  tibble(variable = "AICDA expression", I = aicda$test$estimate[[1]], p = aicda$test$p.value),
  {
    res <- spatialMoran(sirup, variable = "GC B", variable_type = "metadata", k = 6)
    tibble(variable = "GC B cell proportion", I = res$test$estimate[[1]], p = res$test$p.value)
  },
  {
    res <- spatialMoran(sirup, slot = "BCR", variable = "BCR", variable_type = "receptor", k = 6)
    tibble(variable = "BCR present", I = res$test$estimate[[1]], p = res$test$p.value)
  },
  {
    res <- spatialMoran(sirup, slot = "TCR", variable = "TCR", variable_type = "receptor", k = 6)
    tibble(variable = "TCR present", I = res$test$estimate[[1]], p = res$test$p.value)
  }
)
moran_table
```

The GC B cell proportion has a stronger cluster, with $I$ near 0.62. The cell2location estimate is smooth and has no zeros from sampling. A p value of 0 means a value below
the smallest number that R can store.

## Find where a variable is spatially autocorrelated

Global Moran's I gives one number for the whole section. Use `spatialLocalMoran()` to find where a variable is spatially autocorrelated, i.e., which spots sit in a
cluster of similar values. This function computes local Moran's I (also called LISA) for each spot. Local Moran's I is positive when a spot has neighbors with similar
values and negative when a spot differs from its neighbors.

```{r local-moran}
gc_b_local <- spatialLocalMoran(
  sirup,
  variable = "GC B",
  variable_type = "metadata",
  k = 6
)
head(gc_b_local[, c("cell", "value", "local_i", "z_i", "p_value")])
```

`plotSpatialLocalMoran()` draws the z-scores on the tissue. Red spots sit in clusters of similar values, and blue spots differ from their neighbors.

```{r local-moran-plot}
plotSpatialLocalMoran(
  sirup,
  gc_b_local,
  point_size = 1,
  title = "GC B cell proportion, local Moran's I (z-score)"
) +
  guides(color = guide_colorbar(title = "z"))
```

The clusters of high GC B cell proportion sit at the ectopic germinal centers (eGCs). Each spot has its own p value, so correct for multiple testing before calling a spot significant,
e.g., with `p.adjust(method = "BH")`.

## Test whether two variables co-vary in space

Use `spatialLee()` to determine if two continuous variables share a spatial pattern, i.e., if a high value of one variable tends to sit near high values of the other.
This function computes [Lee's L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee%27s_L). Lee's L combines Pearson correlation with spatial smoothing. The variables do not need to peak in
the same spots.

In MG, patients make antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor (AChR). *CHRNA1* codes for the AChR alpha subunit, and thymic myoid cells express it. This test asks
whether *CHRNA1* and the germinal center marker *AICDA* share a spatial pattern. *MS4A1* (CD20) gives a positive control, because GC B cells express both *MS4A1* and *AICDA*.

```{r lee}
lee_control <- spatialLee(
  sirup,
  x = "AICDA", y = "MS4A1",
  assay = "Spatial", layer = "data", k = 6
)
lee_chrna1 <- spatialLee(
  sirup,
  x = "AICDA", y = "CHRNA1",
  assay = "Spatial", layer = "data", k = 6
)

tibble(
  pair = c("AICDA and MS4A1", "AICDA and CHRNA1"),
  L = c(lee_control$L, lee_chrna1$L),
  p = c(lee_control$test$p.value, lee_chrna1$test$p.value)
)
```

The control pair shares a pattern, but *AICDA* and *CHRNA1* do not. In this section, $L$ for that pair is near zero and the test is not significant.

<div markdown="1" style="background: #9e584a; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #8b3620; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Warning</b> </p>
  The analytical test (`method = "analytical"`) builds a dense matrix with one entry for each pair of spots. This works for Visium. For Visium HD, use `method = "mc"`, which uses permutations and sparse weights.
</div>

## Test whether two spot types sit near each other

Use `spatialRipleyCrossK()` to determine if two discrete variables co-vary in space, i.e., if spots of type A lie near spots of type B. This function computes Ripley's
cross K. It counts the spots of type B within each distance of an average spot of type A, then compares that curve with curves from random relabeling of the spots, which gives an
envelope. A curve above the envelope means that A and B sit closer than chance.

T follicular helper (Tfh) cells give B cells the signals that keep a germinal center going. This test asks whether spots with GC B cells sit near spots with Tfh cells.
First, label each spot from its cell2location proportions. `updateSpatial()` runs a function on the Seurat object and stores the result.

```{r ripley-marks}
sirup <- updateSpatial(sirup, function(spatial) {
  gc_b <- spatial$`GC B` > 0.10
  tfh <- spatial$Tfh > 0.10
  spatial$gc_tfh_mark <- case_when(
    gc_b & !tfh ~ "GC B",
    tfh & !gc_b ~ "Tfh",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  )
  spatial
})

table(getSpatial(sirup)$gc_tfh_mark, useNA = "ifany")
```

Spots with neither cell type, or with both, get `NA`, and the test leaves them out. Then run the test. `nsim` sets the number of random relabelings, and 99 or more is
best for a final analysis.

```{r ripley, eval = has_spatstat, results = "hide"}
gc_tfh_k <- spatialRipleyCrossK(
  sirup,
  mark_col = "gc_tfh_mark",
  i = "GC B",
  j = "Tfh",
  nsim = 39,
  max_r = 40
)

plotRipleyCrossK(gc_tfh_k, title = "Cross K: GC B spots to Tfh spots")
```

In this section, the observed curve lies below the envelope at every distance. Random relabeling keeps the marked spots in place and shuffles the labels, so a curve below
the envelope means that GC B spots sit next to other GC B spots more often than next to Tfh spots. The same holds for Tfh spots. The two cell types form separate groups at the
10% threshold. The rule that drops spots with both cell types adds to the separation, so change the thresholds or the marks to ask a different question.

The distance $r$ is in image pixels at the stored `image_scale`. To convert it to micrometers, use the Visium spot size. A spot is 55 µm wide, and the image object stores the spot
diameter in full-resolution pixels:

```{r microns, eval = has_spatstat}
scale_factors <- getSpatial(sirup)@images[[1]]@scale.factors
um_per_pixel <- 55 / (scale_factors$spot * scale_factors$lowres)
um_per_pixel
max(gc_tfh_k$plot_data$r) * um_per_pixel
```

The value `max_r = 40` lowres pixels is about 470 µm.

## Test whether a clone is spatially autocorrelated

Use `spatialCloneJoinCount()` to determine if the spots of one clone sit next to each other. This function computes the
[join count statistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Join_count_statistic). It marks the spots that have the clone, counts the neighbor pairs in which both spots have the clone
(the joins), and compares that count with the count expected by chance. If the clone stays in one place, the section has more joins than random labeling gives.

The function tests each clone that occurs in at least `min_spatial_ids` spots. If the object has stored polygons, it runs one test for each polygon by default. Set
`use_stored_polygons = FALSE` for one test over the whole section.

```{r join-count}
big_clones <- getReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR") %>%
  filter(!is.na(barcode_10x)) %>%
  distinct(clone_id, barcode_10x) %>%
  count(clone_id, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  pull(clone_id)

join_count <- spatialCloneJoinCount(
  sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  clone_val = big_clones,
  use_stored_polygons = FALSE,
  k = 6,
  return_data = TRUE
)

join_count$summary
```

The summary has one row for each clone. `statistic` is the standardized join count (a z-score) and `p_value` is the one-sided p value. `plotSpatialCloneJoinCount()` shows
the clone and its joins. The plot needs `return_data = TRUE` in the test.

```{r join-count-plot}
plotSpatialCloneJoinCount(
  join_count = join_count,
  object = sirup,
  clone_val = join_count$summary$clone_id[[1]],
  show_neighbors = TRUE
)
```

## Measure how far a clone spreads

Use `spatialCloneSpread()` to describe how far each clone reaches across the section. This function is descriptive, so it does not report a test. It uses the
pairwise distances between the sequences of the clone.

```{r spread}
spread <- spatialCloneSpread(sirup, slot = "BCR", min_spatial_ids = 3)
spread %>%
  arrange(desc(n_spatial_ids)) %>%
  head()
```

The table gives the mean and the maximum pairwise distance for each clone, in image pixels. By default, sequences in the same spot count as separate points at
distance 0. Set `collapse_within_spot = TRUE` to count each spot once.

## Save the results in the object

Store the results in the object with `setAnalysis()`, so they travel with the data.

```{r store}
sirup <- sirup %>%
  setAnalysis("moran_aicda", aicda) %>%
  setAnalysis("local_moran_gc_b", gc_b_local) %>%
  setAnalysis("lee_aicda_chrna1", lee_chrna1) %>%
  setAnalysis("clone_join_count", join_count) %>%
  setAnalysis("clone_spread", spread)
listAnalyses(sirup)
```
